cse-2020-cs-35.approach: Simulate SSTF: from the current head position always pick the pending request with the smallest seek distance. Then test each statement against the service order.
cse-2020-cs-35.given:
| Request | P | Q | R | S | T |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cylinder | 155 | 85 | 110 | 30 | 115 |

Head starts at cylinder 100.

steps.title: From 100
steps.body: Distances: P 55, Q 15, R 10, S 70, T 15. Nearest is **R (110)**, moving up.

steps.title: From 110
steps.body: Distances: P 45, Q 25, S 80, T 5. Nearest is **T (115)**, still moving up.

steps.title: From 115
steps.body: Distances: P $155-115=40$, Q $115-85=30$, S $115-30=85$. Nearest is **Q (85)** — the head reverses and moves down.

steps.title: From 85, then 30
steps.body:
Distances: P $155-85=70$, S $85-30=55$. Serve **S (30)** (still down), then the only one left, **P (155)**, so the head reverses again.

Order: **R, T, Q, S, P**.

scene.caption: Order R, T, Q, S, P

steps.title: Check the statements
steps.body:
- (A) T (2nd) before P (5th): true.
- (B) Q (3rd) is serviced **before** S (4th), not after: **false**.
- (C) After Q the head goes down to S and then turns up to P: it reverses, true.
- (D) R (1st) before P: true.

optionAnalysis.reason: True: T is served 2nd, P last.
False statement: Q (3rd) is served before S (4th), so "Q after S" is wrong.
True: between Q and P the head goes down to S and then turns back up.
True: R is served first.

pitfalls: Q (85) and T (115) are both 15 from 100, but R at 110 is nearer still, so neither is the first pick.
cse-2020-cs-35.verification: Total seek $10+5+30+55+125=225$; at every step the chosen request had the strictly smallest distance, so there were no ties to break.

cse-2020-cs-36.approach: BCNF needs every nontrivial FD to have a superkey on the left. 3NF also allows X → A when A is prime. So a table in 3NF but not BCNF must have exactly that extra kind of FD.

steps.title: Not BCNF
steps.body: Some nontrivial FD $X \rightarrow A$ has $X$ **not** a superkey.

steps.title: Yet in 3NF
steps.body:
3NF allows $X \rightarrow A$ with $X$ not a superkey only when $A$ is a **prime** attribute (part of some candidate key). So that violating FD must have $A$ prime — statement (A).

Example: $R(A,B,C)$ with $AB \rightarrow C$, $C \rightarrow B$: keys $AB$, $AC$; $C \rightarrow B$ has $C$ not a superkey but $B$ prime.

optionAnalysis.reason: This is exactly the FD that 3NF permits but BCNF forbids.
Non-key X determining a non-prime A (transitive dependency) violates 3NF.
Part of a key determining a non-prime attribute is a partial dependency — it violates 2NF, hence 3NF.
A set-valued cell violates 1NF, so R could not be in 3NF.

pitfalls: 3NF is a relaxation of BCNF only for prime right-hand sides.
cse-2020-cs-36.verification: The example $R(A,B,C)$, $AB\rightarrow C$, $C\rightarrow B$ is in 3NF (B is prime) but not in BCNF ($C$ is not a superkey).

cse-2020-cs-37.approach: Two schedules are conflict equivalent iff they order every conflicting pair (same item, different transactions, at least one write) the same way. List the conflicting pairs of the given schedule and check each option.
cse-2020-cs-37.given: Given order: $R_1A,\ R_2B,\ W_2B,\ R_1C,\ R_2D,\ W_1D,\ W_2C,\ W_1B$, then both commit.

steps.title: Conflicting pairs
steps.body:
- On $B$: $R_2B$ and $W_2B$ come before $W_1B$ ⇒ $T_2$ before $T_1$ on $B$.
- On $C$: $R_1C$ before $W_2C$ ⇒ $T_1$ before $T_2$ on $C$.
- On $D$: $R_2D$ before $W_1D$ ⇒ $T_2$ before $T_1$ on $D$.
- $A$ is touched only by $T_1$: no conflict.

(The precedence graph has a cycle, so no **serial** schedule can be equivalent — options B and D are serial.)

steps.title: Test each option
steps.body:
- (A) $R_2B, W_2B, R_2D$ first, then $R_1A, R_1C, W_1D, W_1B$, then $W_2C$: $B$ ✓, $D$ ✓, and $R_1C$ precedes $W_2C$ ✓.
- (B) $W_1B$ before $R_2B$ and $W_1D$ before $R_2D$ ✗.
- (C) $W_1D$ (3rd) before $R_2D$ ✗.
- (D) $W_2C$ before $R_1C$ ✗.

optionAnalysis.reason: Keeps T2 before T1 on B and D, and T1 before T2 on C.
Serial T1 T2: W1B precedes R2B/W2B and W1D precedes R2D, reversing two conflicts.
W1D is executed before R2D, reversing the conflict on D.
Serial T2 T1: W2C precedes R1C, reversing the conflict on C.

pitfalls: The given schedule is not conflict serializable (cycle T1→T2→T1), so the serial options cannot be right.
cse-2020-cs-37.verification: Option A can also be reached from the given schedule by swapping only adjacent non-conflicting operations (e.g. moving R1A and R1C after R2D, which touch different items).

cse-2020-cs-38.approach: 1500 hosts need a /21 block (2048 addresses). A valid candidate must be a properly aligned /21 (third octet a multiple of 8) lying inside the ISP's 202.61.0.0/17.

steps.title: Block size
steps.body: $2^{10}=1024 < 1500 \le 2^{11}=2048$, so the organization needs 11 host bits: a **/21**. A /21 spans $2^{3}=8$ values of the third octet, so its third octet must be a multiple of 8.

steps.title: ISP range
steps.body: /17 fixes the first bit of the third octet: 202.61.0.0/17 covers **202.61.0.0 – 202.61.127.255** (third octet 0–127).

optionAnalysis.reason: 202.61.84.0 is not a /21 boundary (84 is not a multiple of 8).
II and III are aligned /21 blocks inside 202.61.0.0/17.
202.61.144.0 is outside the /17 (third octet must be ≤ 127).
I is misaligned and IV is outside the ISP space.

pitfalls: A block like 84.0/21 would have host bits set in its network address — it is not a legal prefix.
cse-2020-cs-38.verification: 104 = 01101000 and 64 = 01000000 have the leading bit 0 (inside /17) and the low 3 bits 000 (aligned to /21).

cse-2020-cs-39.approach: Rewrite each implication as a disjunction and move the quantifier past W (which has no free x). The only formula that does not survive this is the ∀ with an implication.

steps.title: Pull W out
steps.body:
Because $x$ is not free in $W$:
- $\forall x(p(x)\vee W) \equiv \forall x\,p(x)\vee W$ — (A) valid.
- $\exists x(p(x)\wedge W) \equiv \exists x\,p(x)\wedge W$ — (B) valid.

steps.title: Implications
steps.body:
$ orall x(p(x)ightarrow W) \equiv  orall x(
eg p(x)\vee W) \equiv ( orall x\,
eg p(x))\vee W \equiv 
eg\exists x\,p(x)\vee W \equiv \exists x\,p(x)ightarrow W$.

So the correct right side of (C) is $\exists x\,p(x)ightarrow W$, not $ orall x\,p(x)ightarrow W$.

$\exists x(p(x)ightarrow W) \equiv \exists x\,
eg p(x)\vee W \equiv 
eg orall x\,p(x)\vee W \equiv  orall x\,p(x)ightarrow W$ — (D) valid.

steps.title: Counterexample for (C)
steps.body:
Domain $\{1,2\}$, $p(1)=\text{T}$, $p(2)=\text{F}$, $W=\text{F}$.
- Left: $p(1)\rightarrow \text{F}$ is false, so $\forall x(p(x)\rightarrow W)$ is **false**.
- Right: $\forall x\,p(x)$ is false, so $\forall x\,p(x)\rightarrow W$ is **true**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Valid: ∀ distributes over ∨ with a constant (x-free) disjunct.
Valid: ∃ distributes over ∧ with an x-free conjunct.
Not valid: ∀x(p(x)→W) ≡ ∃x p(x) → W; the counterexample separates the two sides.
Valid: ∃x(¬p(x) ∨ W) ≡ ¬∀x p(x) ∨ W ≡ ∀x p(x) → W.

cse-2020-cs-39.shortcut: A quantifier flips (∀↔∃) when it is pulled out of the antecedent of an implication.
pitfalls: Pulling a quantifier out of the left side of → changes it, because the antecedent is negated.
cse-2020-cs-39.verification: The counterexample makes the two sides of (C) differ; (A), (B), (D) follow by standard equivalences.

cse-2020-cs-40.approach: Sum w' along any path: the f-terms telescope, leaving only f(start) − f(end). Every path between the same two vertices shifts by the same constant, so shortest paths are preserved for any f.

steps.title: Telescope
steps.body:
For a path $v_0 \to v_1 \to \dots \to v_k$:
$$w'(P)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\big(w(v_{i-1},v_i)+f(v_{i-1})-f(v_i)\big)=w(P)+f(v_0)-f(v_k).$$

steps.title: Same shift for all u–v paths
steps.body: For fixed endpoints $u,v$, every path gets the same added constant $f(u)-f(v)$. The order of path lengths is unchanged, so a shortest path under $w$ is a shortest path under $w'$ — **for every** $f$ (cycle weights are unchanged too, so negative cycles neither appear nor vanish).

optionAnalysis.reason: The telescoping sum shows the property holds for any f.
"If and only if" is wrong: f need not be positive.
Negative f works, but so does any other f, so "only if" fails.
That is Johnson's choice, which additionally makes w' non-negative; it is sufficient, not necessary.

pitfalls: Confusing preservation of shortest paths (any f) with making weights non-negative (needs Johnson's specific f).
cse-2020-cs-40.verification: Check: path s→a→t vs s→t with any f: both get the same added constant f(s) − f(t), so their difference is unchanged.

cse-2020-cs-41.approach: Search for a and b down the balanced tree (O(log n)), then output every key between them by an in-order walk, which touches O(k) more nodes.

steps.title: Locate the boundaries
steps.body: Descending from the root to where $a$ (and $b$) would be costs the tree height, $\Theta(\log n)$ — needed even when $k=0$.

steps.title: Report the range
steps.body: All nodes off the two boundary paths that are visited lie inside $[a,b]$, so the in-order traversal between them costs $O(k)$. Total worst case: $\Theta(\log n + k)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Ignores the cost of outputting k elements (k can be Θ(n)).
Θ(log n) to find the boundary plus Θ(k) to report.
That is k independent searches; the in-order walk avoids it.
Unrelated to the work done; overestimates for small k.

cse-2020-cs-41.verification: Extremes: k = 0 needs one root-to-leaf path, Θ(log n); k = n needs a full traversal, Θ(n) — both match Θ(log n + k).

cse-2020-cs-42.approach: Place the two identical L's first: they cannot sit at positions 1 or 3, so they take two of positions {2, 4, 5}. Then count arrangements of I, A, C in the remaining three positions avoiding their own spots.

steps.title: Place the L's
steps.body: L's must avoid 1 and 3, so they occupy 2 of $\{2,4,5\}$: $\binom{3}{2}=3$ cases. In each case exactly one of I, A, C still has its own position free.

steps.title: Fill I, A, C
steps.body: The 3 free positions are $\{1,3,x\}$ where $x$ is the original position of one letter. Arrangements of 3 letters: $3!=6$; those putting that letter on $x$: $2!=2$. Valid: $6-2=4$ per case.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: Each of the 3 placements of the L's leaves exactly 4 valid fillings, so the total is $3 \times 4 = 12$.

pitfalls: Treating the L's as distinct (and dividing at the end) is error-prone; place them as a pair instead.
cse-2020-cs-42.verification: Case L at {4,5}: positions 1,2,3 for I,A,C with I≠2 → IAC, ICA, ACI, CAI → 4 (AIC and CIA put I back at 2), consistent with 4.

cse-2020-cs-43.approach: Compare average time per instruction. Non-pipelined: 5 cycles at 2.5 GHz. Pipelined: ideal CPI 1 plus stall cycles per instruction, at 2 GHz.

steps.title: Non-pipelined
steps.body: Cycle time $= 1/2.5\text{ GHz} = 0.4$ ns; time per instruction $= 5 \times 0.4 = 2$ ns.

steps.title: Pipelined CPI
steps.body:
Stalls per instruction:
- memory: $0.30 \times 0.05 \times 50 = 0.75$
- branch: $0.10 \times 0.50 \times 2 = 0.1$

CPI $= 1 + 0.75 + 0.1 = 1.85$. Cycle time $= 1/2\text{ GHz} = 0.5$ ns, so time per instruction $= 1.85 \times 0.5 = 0.925$ ns.

pitfalls: Using the same clock for both processors (would give 5/1.85 = 2.70).
Branches are 100 − 30 − 60 = 10% of instructions.

cse-2020-cs-44.approach: Count the 16-bit encoding space. Each I-type opcode uses up all patterns of its 10 operand bits; each R-type opcode uses all patterns of its 12 operand bits. Whatever space the I-types leave is shared by R-types.

steps.title: Operand fields
steps.body:
64 registers ⇒ 6-bit register field.
- I-type: $6 + 4 = 10$ operand bits ⇒ opcode bits $= 16-10 = 6$.
- R-type: $6+6 = 12$ operand bits ⇒ opcode bits $= 16-12 = 4$.

steps.title: Share the space
steps.body:
Total encodings $2^{16}$. Each R-type opcode occupies $2^{12}$ encodings, so the 4-bit opcode field has $2^4=16$ slots. 8 I-type opcodes need $8 \times 2^{10} = 2^{13} = 2 \times 2^{12}$ encodings, i.e. 2 of those slots.

Maximum R-type opcodes $= 16 - 2 = \mathbf{14}$.

pitfalls: Answering 16 − 8 = 8 forgets that one 4-bit R-slot, extended by 2 more bits, holds 4 I-type opcodes.

cse-2020-cs-45.approach: Since a ≠ 0, pick an index j with a_j = 1. Fixing all other bits of x, flipping x_j flips the parity of the sum, so exactly half of all x give an odd sum.

steps.title: Pair the vectors
steps.body: Let $a_j=1$. Pair each $x$ with $x'$ that differs only in bit $j$. Then $\sum a_i x'_i = \sum a_i x_i \pm 1$, so exactly one of the pair has an odd sum.

steps.title: Probability
steps.body: The $2^n$ vectors split into $2^{n-1}$ pairs, each contributing one odd sum: $P = \dfrac{2^{n-1}}{2^n} = \mathbf{0.5}$.

pitfalls: The answer does not depend on how many 1s a has, only that it has at least one.
cse-2020-cs-45.verification: n = 3, a = (1,1,0): odd sum when x₁ ≠ x₂, which is 4 of 8 vectors = 0.5.

cse-2020-cs-46.approach: Both functions use static counters that are never reset. fun1(n) adds n to its counter and returns the running total; fun2 accumulates those totals for n = 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.

steps.title: What fun1 does
steps.body: `fun1(n)` increments its static `i` once per level, i.e. $n$ times, then returns the current `i`. Because `i` persists, each call returns the **cumulative** count.

steps.title: Return value
steps.body: Every `fun2` level returns the static `i` after the deeper calls finish, so `fun2(5)` returns **55**.

pitfalls: Treating i in fun1 as resetting each call gives 5+4+3+2+1 = 15.

cse-2020-cs-47.approach: In a min-heap the maximum must be a leaf (any internal node is smaller than its child). So find the max among the leaves only.

steps.title: Count leaves
steps.body: With $n=1023$ nodes, internal nodes are indices $1..\lfloor n/2\rfloor = 1..511$; leaves are $512..1023$: $1023-511 = 512$ leaves.

steps.title: Max of 512 items
steps.body: The leaves are unordered among themselves, and finding the max of $m$ unordered elements needs $m-1$ comparisons: $512 - 1 = \mathbf{511}$.

pitfalls: Scanning all 1023 elements (1022 comparisons) is not minimal.
cse-2020-cs-47.verification: 1023 = 2¹⁰ − 1 is a complete tree with 10 levels; the last level holds 2⁹ = 512 leaves.

cse-2020-cs-48.approach: tob stores the binary digits of b (LSB first); pp is square-and-multiply, so pp(a, b) = a^b. Trace it for b = 4.

steps.title: Loop in pp
steps.body:
Start tot $=1$, ex $=3$.
- $i=0$: arr 0, tot stays 1; ex $=9$.
- $i=1$: arr 0, tot stays 1; ex $=81$.
- $i=2$: arr 1, tot $=1 \times 81 = 81$; ex $=6561$.

pitfalls: tot is multiplied by ex *before* ex is squared in the same iteration.

cse-2020-cs-49.approach: Every edge weighs at least 1 and a spanning tree on 100 vertices has 99 edges, so the weight is at least 99. The path v1–v2–…–v100 uses only weight-1 edges, reaching that bound.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: Any spanning tree has $100-1 = 99$ edges, each of weight $|i-j| \ge 1$, so weight $\ge 99$.

steps.title: Achieve it
steps.body: Edges $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ for $i=1..99$ all have weight 1 and form a path through all vertices — a spanning tree of weight $99 \times 1 = \mathbf{99}$.

cse-2020-cs-49.verification: Kruskal picks the 99 weight-1 edges first; they connect everything without a cycle, so no heavier edge is needed.

cse-2020-cs-50.approach: All arrive at 0, so turnaround time = completion time. Draw both Gantt charts, average the completion times, and subtract.

steps.title: SJF
steps.body:
Order by burst: P3 (2), P4 (4), P2 (7), P1 (8). Completions: P3 = 2, P4 = 6, P2 = 13, P1 = 21.

Average TAT $= \dfrac{2+6+13+21}{4} = \dfrac{42}{4} = 10.5$ ms.

pitfalls: In RR, P3 and P4 finish within their first quantum, so P1 and P2 come back at 14 and 18.
cse-2020-cs-50.verification: Both schedules end at 21 = 8 + 7 + 2 + 4 ms, as they must with no idle time.

cse-2020-cs-51.approach: Divisibility by 2 and by 3 together depend only on (#a mod 6). Build the mod-6 counter on a's, accept residues 2 and 4, and check that all six states are distinguishable.

steps.title: Accepting residues
steps.body: Let $c = \#a \bmod 6$. Divisible by 2: $c \in \{0,2,4\}$; divisible by 3: $c \in \{0,3\}$. So accept $c \in \{2,4\}$ ($c=0$ is divisible by both, so it is rejected).

steps.title: Mod-6 DFA
steps.body: States $q_0..q_5$; on $a$ go $q_c \to q_{(c+1)\bmod 6}$; on $b$ stay. Accepting: $q_2, q_4$.

steps.title: All 6 distinguishable
steps.body: From $q_r$, the suffix $a^k$ is accepted iff $(r+k) \bmod 6 \in \{2,4\}$. Two states $q_r \neq q_s$ are equivalent only if $\{2,4\}$ is unchanged by the shift $s-r$; shifts 1..5 give $\{3,5\},\{4,0\},\{5,1\},\{0,2\},\{1,3\}$ — none equals $\{2,4\}$. So no two states merge: minimum = **6**.

pitfalls: Accepting zero a's by mistake: 0 is divisible by 3, so the start state must be rejecting.
Counting only the mod-2 condition (2 states) ignores the mod-3 exclusion.
cse-2020-cs-51.verification: Product of a mod-2 and a mod-3 counter also has 2 × 3 = 6 states, matching the mod-6 counter (CRT).

cse-2020-cs-52.approach: The chromatic index is at least Δ(G) = deg(s) = 7. Exhibit a 7-edge-colouring: 4-colour K₃,₄ so that the four degree-3 vertices each miss a different colour, then colour s's edges.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: $s$ is adjacent to all $3+4=7$ vertices, so $\Delta(G)=7$ and at least 7 colours are needed. (Other degrees: $4+1=5$ and $3+1=4$.)

steps.title: Colour K₃,₄ with 4 colours
steps.body: Let $u_0,u_1,u_2$ and $v_0..v_3$ be the parts; colour $(u_i,v_j)$ with $(i+j) \bmod 4$. Each $u_i$ sees all 4 colours (distinct $j$). Vertex $v_j$ sees $j, j+1, j+2 \pmod 4$ and **misses** $(j+3)\bmod 4$ — a different colour for each $j$.

steps.title: Colour the edges at s
steps.body: Give $(s,v_j)$ the colour $v_j$ misses: four distinct colours from $\{0,1,2,3\}$. Give $(s,u_0),(s,u_1),(s,u_2)$ new colours 4, 5, 6. No conflicts, so 7 colours suffice: answer **7**.

pitfalls: Vizing only bounds the answer by 7 or 8; a construction is needed to rule out 8.
cse-2020-cs-52.verification: Edge count 12 + 7 = 19; with 7 colours and 8 vertices each colour class is a matching of at most 4 edges, so capacity 28 ≥ 19 — no counting obstruction, and the explicit colouring works.

cse-2020-cs-53.approach: TLB is checked on every access. On a TLB hit one memory access follows. On a TLB miss the page table is read from memory; with probability 0.1 that reference faults, costing the disk transfer(s) before the access.
cse-2020-cs-53.given:
| TLB | Memory | Disk transfer | TLB hit | Fault rate | Dirty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 ns | 100 ns | 5000 ns | 0.95 | 0.10 | 0.20 |

steps.title: TLB miss
steps.body:
$20$ (TLB) $+ 100$ (page table) then:
- no fault (0.9): one memory access, $100$;
- fault (0.1): read page $5000$, plus write-back $5000$ with probability $0.2$, then the access $100$: $5000 + 0.2\times 5000 + 100 = 6100$.

Miss time $= 120 + 0.9\times100 + 0.1\times6100 = 120 + 90 + 610 = 820$ ns.

pitfalls: Applying the 10% fault rate to every access (including TLB hits) gives about 725 ns; a TLB hit means the page is resident.

cse-2020-cs-54.approach: Minimum accesses means the shallowest tree, i.e. nodes as full as possible. Compute the max fan-out from the 4 KB block, find the number of levels needed for 10⁶ keys, and add one access for the data block.

steps.title: Node capacities
steps.body:
Internal node with $p$ pointers: $8p + 12(p-1) \le 4096 \Rightarrow 20p \le 4108 \Rightarrow p = 205$.
Leaf with $k$ (key, record pointer) pairs plus a next-leaf pointer: $20k + 8 \le 4096 \Rightarrow k = 204$.

steps.title: Levels
steps.body:
Leaves: $\lceil 10^6/204 \rceil = 4902$.
Next level: $\lceil 4902/205 \rceil = 24$ nodes.
Root: $24 \le 205$, so one node.
Height = 3 levels (root, 24 internal, 4902 leaves).

steps.title: Accesses
steps.body: 3 index blocks + 1 data block $= \mathbf{4}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the final access to the record's own block gives 3.
cse-2020-cs-54.verification: Two index levels cover only $205 \times 204 = 41820 < 10^6$ records, so 3 index levels are necessary, and $205^2 \times 204 \approx 8.6\times10^6 \ge 10^6$ shows 3 suffice.

cse-2020-cs-55.approach: Start with cwnd = 1 MSS = 2 KB. Slow start doubles cwnd every RTT (6 ms) until it reaches ssthresh = 32 KB; after that congestion avoidance adds 1 MSS per RTT. Count RTTs up to 60 ms.

steps.title: Slow start
steps.body: $t=0$: 2 KB; 6 ms: 4; 12 ms: 8; 18 ms: 16; 24 ms: 32 KB = ssthresh.

steps.title: Receiver window
steps.body: 44 KB < 50 KB (advertised window), so the receiver window does not cap it. Answer: **44**.

pitfalls: Continuing to double past ssthresh.
Capping at 50 KB too early — the window never reaches it by 60 ms.
cse-2020-cs-55.verification: 60/6 = 10 RTTs: 4 doublings (2→32) then 6 increments of 2 KB: 32 + 12 = 44.
